The authors address a critical gap in the field by focusing on the ability of MLFFs to extrapolate to out-of-distribution (OOD) data, a crucial requirement for their practical application in molecular discovery and materials science. The benchmark consists of four distinct tasks, each targeting a specific aspect of compositional generalization: length extrapolation, functional group composition, functional group duplication, and functional group combination. These tasks are designed to challenge MLFFs by systematically altering molecular structures, such as varying chain lengths and combining different functional groups. The authors generated the benchmark dataset using the GFN2-xTB method, ensuring high-fidelity energy and force labels. They then evaluated five state-of-the-art MLFF architectures on GMD-25, revealing a significant performance degradation on OOD samples compared to in-distribution (ID) data. This finding highlights a critical limitation of current MLFFs, indicating that even advanced models struggle to generalize to chemically novel molecules. The authors' approach involves creating OOD test sets by modifying the structure of molecules, which is a more direct and relevant test of generalization than simply using molecules not seen during training. The empirical results demonstrate that current MLFFs, despite their success on in-distribution data, often fail to generalize to even slightly modified chemical structures.
